title: Present perfect: experiences
objectives: Form present perfect statements and questions about experiences.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: The present perfect connects a past action or experience with the present. One common use is to talk about something that has happened at least once in a person's life up to now, without saying exactly when. ‘I have visited Scotland’ tells us about my experience; the listener does not learn the date. The time period considered is my life up to the present.

We often use ever in questions about life experience: ‘Have you ever tried sushi?’ Never means ‘not at any time’ in the relevant period: ‘I have never tried sushi’. We can use before or expressions such as once and twice when the exact date is not the focus.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Make the present perfect with have or has plus the past participle. Use have with I, you, we and they, and has with he, she, it and a singular noun. For many regular verbs, the past participle ends in -ed: visited, played and watched. Many common participles are irregular: been, seen, eaten, taken, written and done.

Make a negative with have not or haven't, and has not or hasn't: ‘She hasn't seen the film’. Put have or has before the subject in a question: ‘Have they been to London?’ A short answer uses the auxiliary: ‘Yes, they have’ or ‘No, they haven't’. In informal English, ‘I've’ and ‘she's’ can mean ‘I have’ and ‘she has’ here.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Read the examples below. ‘Have you ever ridden a horse?’ asks about experience at any time in your life up to now. ‘Yes, I have’ answers the question. A follow-up can use the past simple to give a finished time: ‘I rode one on holiday last year’. The first question focuses on experience; the second sentence tells us when it happened.

In British English, ‘have been to’ often describes a visit and return: ‘I've been to Lisbon twice’. ‘Has gone to Lisbon’ usually means the person has left for Lisbon and is not here now. For a life-experience question about visiting a place, been to is often the form we need.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not add a separate negative to never in standard English: say ‘I have never seen it’, not ‘I haven't never seen it’. Do not use the present perfect with a finished past time such as yesterday or in 2019 in this experience pattern: say ‘I saw it yesterday’. The next units explore time references in more detail.

A past participle is not always the same as the past simple form. For example, saw is the past simple of see, but seen is its past participle. Say ‘I saw it last week’ and ‘I have seen it’. Some verbs have the same form for both, such as visited; check irregular forms when necessary.

examples.note: The exact dates are not stated.

common_errors.reason: Use the participle seen after has.
Use the participle eaten after have.
He takes has in the question.

summary: Use have or has plus a past participle for experiences up to now.
Use ever in questions and never for no experience.
Use the past simple when a finished past time is stated.
